topic: Understanding the Failure of Novel MEMS Microplasma Reactors
title: Understanding the Failure of Novel MEMS Microplasma Reactors
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering
authors_text: Eugene Bender and Peter Lindner
abstract: Compact fuel cells are the logical progression for portable power as they have much higher energy densities than battery technology. However, fuel cells have not dominated the portable power market as they require a readily available source of hydrogen. Hydrogen gas is generally produced at large scale steam reforming plants. Transporting the hydrogen from these plants is impractical for portable applications due to its large volume even when compressed. Instead a better option is to produce the hydrogen locally and create a fuel reformer-fuel cell system. Micro-reactors offer the unique advantages of being able to process hydrocarbons adjacent to a fuel cell. Microplasma reactors developed from standard semiconductor fabrication techniques have been tested in reforming various hydrocarbons. Plasmas were used as the reaction media as they have many advantages over common catalytic reactions. In contrast to conventional catalytic reactions, plasmas have instantaneous startup times, can operate at room temperatures, and eliminate the possibility of sulfur poisoning and coking. The microplasma reactors analyzed in this study were microhollow cathode discharge (MHCD) devices. The reactors each have three key layers to produce a plasma. The three layers are an n-doped silicon cathode, a silicon dioxide dielectric, and a nickel/titanium anode. The silicon has a trench etched into it where the plasma reaction occurs. A high voltage (~500V) is established across the anode and cathode to develop the plasma in the trench. 36 variations of reactors were fabricated, with deviations in the oxide thickness (2, 4 μm), trench depth (25, 100, 250 μm), trench width (25, 100, 250 μm), and with and without a patterned anode. Experiments with these reactors were successful in showing the feasibility of a portable microplasma fuel reformer, but the devices regularly had lifetime issues. Devices would stop working with in an operation time of a few seconds to a few hours. The inconsistency as well as short lifetime pressed an investigation to why these reactors fail. The electrical and physical properties of the thirteen failed microplasma reactors have been investigated with the goal of determining what caused their malfunction. These devices have been tested by recording their electrical characteristics under loads ranging from -20 to 20 volts. Then they were imaged using an optical microscope as well as a scanning electron microscope (SEM) to determine the point of failure. Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) was used to identify the distribution of elements in the channel, anode surface, and cross-section of the microreactor. Devices that hadn’t performed a reaction were also investigated in the same manner as the failed thirteen reactors. Preliminary SEM imaging suggests a number of chemical and physical changes occurring during the operation of these reactors. The most prominent of these occurrences was the formation or re-deposition of silicon and silicon dioxide on the inner walls of the microchannel. Further inspection using EDS revealed that the nickel anode was also dispersed throughout the channel, indicating an electrical bridge is likely being developed from the cathode to the anode. Further investigation of the reactors is required to determine if the deposition of these materials is a function of the device dimensions, system parameters (reactants, products, flow rates, etc.), and/or the power applied during the plasma reaction. This analysis will enable us to improve on the design of the microplasma reactor and furthermore allow for the development of a portable fuel reformer-fuel cell system.

topic: Looped Oxide Catalysis: The Prospect of Bio Oil Deoxygenation over Reduced Metal Oxides
title: Looped Oxide Catalysis: The Prospect of Bio Oil Deoxygenation over Reduced Metal Oxides
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering
authors_text: Cory Hargus, Ronald Michalsky and Andrew A. Peterson
abstract: One of the key challenges in the production of liquid transportation fuels from cellulosic biomass is the upgrading of primary bioliquids to reduce the total oxygen content. This upgrading step is necessary to generate fuels with higher combustion energy, volatility and thermal stability and lower viscosity and molecular weight. Hydrodeoxygenation (HDO) of biomass fast-pyrolysis and liquefaction bio-oils with renewably-sourced H 2 represents a promising carbon-neutral upgrading pathway. However, HDO processing is limited by requisite high pressures and by the destruction of chemical exergy during the reaction of H­ 2 with easily-reduced oxygenate compounds. As an alternative to HDO, we propose a two-step thermochemical cycle wherein a metal oxide is reduced to its metal or to a lower-valence oxide in a high-temperature solar furnace and subsequently reacted with a bio-oil feedstock, reforming the higher oxide and yielding a deoxygenated fuel product. This process, which we have termed “looped oxide catalysis” (LOC), synthesizes concepts from the fields of solar thermochemical hydrogen production, chemical looping, and hydroprocessing and may allow for low-pressure deoxygenation of bio-oil while also achieving high exergy efficiency. From a set of eighty possible LOC catalysts we have identified five most-promising candidates on the basis of known diffusion kinetics, catalytic activity in HDO reactions, and metal-oxygen bond strength. Oxides with low metal-oxygen bond strength will be unable to abstract oxygen from bio-oil oxygenates, while oxides with high metal-oxygen bond strength will require excess energy to reduce. Therefore oxides with intermediate metal-oxygen bond strength are most desirable; this behavior is illustrated in a thermodynamic “volcano plot.” An exergy analysis of the LOC cycle is developed for the five candidate oxides to identify inherent thermodynamic irreversibilities. Additionally, the experimental performance of the five candidate LOC catalysts in a continuous-flow reactor will be discussed in comparison with traditional HDO catalysts.

topic: Effect of Promoter Deposition Order on Platinum-, Ruthenium-, and Rhenium-Promoted Cobalt Fischer-Tropsch Catalysts
title: Effect of Promoter Deposition Order on Platinum-, Ruthenium-, and Rhenium-Promoted Cobalt Fischer-Tropsch Catalysts
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering
authors_text: Hector Perez, Kari M. Cook and William C Hecker
abstract: Abstract The effects of noble metal (NM) promoter (Pt, Re, or Ru) deposition order were investigated in commercially-representative Co Fischer-Tropsch catalysts (nominally 25 wt% Co on a La stabilized alumina support). The effects of deposition sequence (co-deposition vs. sequential deposition) were studied in terms of NM retention and distribution, Co crystallite size, Co reducibility, and catalyst activity and selectivity. Ru retention was <48% with more severe losses for co-deposition (85% loss). Sequentially deposited Co/Ru showed poor Ru distribution, unlike co-deposited Co/Ru. Excellent retention and uniform distribution were observed for both Pt and Re promoted catalysts. Cobalt crystallite sizes were smaller for all three co-deposited catalysts (~4.2 nm for all NMs) when compared to any of the sequentially deposited catalysts. Although sequentially deposited catalysts required higher reduction temperatures (TPR), they had greater extents of reduction (EORs) relative to co-deposited catalysts. CO depletion rates and turnover frequencies (TOFs) for co-deposited Co/Pt and Co/Re were 2-3 times higher than their sequentially deposited counterparts. Methane selectivities were lower for co-deposited Co/Pt and Co/Re. It is interesting to note that the smaller Co crystallite sizes (co-deposition) resulted in more active catalysts than those with larger crystallites (sequentially deposition), which is counter to previous work on unpromoted Co catalysts. The co-deposited Co/Pt catalyst was found to be statistically more active than the unpromoted Co catalyst, while the corresponding sequentially deposited catalyst was less active. Overall, co-deposited Co/Pt and Co/Re catalysts showed superior catalytic performance by all standards of judgment when compared to their sequentially deposited counterparts.

topic: Quantification of Hydrogen and Oxygen Production to Assess Selectivity of Electrocatalysts for Solar Water Splitting
title: Quantification of Hydrogen and Oxygen Production to Assess Selectivity of Electrocatalysts for Solar Water Splitting
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering
authors_text: Kara Fong, Jesse D. Benck, Thomas R. Hellstern and Thomas F. Jaramillo
abstract: Photoelectrochemical water splitting presents an environmentally friendly means of producing hydrogen for use as fuel or industrial feedstock; current research in this field primarily focuses on developing the ideal catalysts and semiconductors for this process. It is undesirable for a given electrocatalyst/semiconductor pair to have less than 100% faradaic efficiency for the solar water splitting reaction, which literature has shown may occur through unwanted side reactions or catalyst/semiconductor degradation. A technique is developed to quantify the production of hydrogen and oxygen in a photoelectrochemical cell in order to assess the faradaic efficiency of electrocatalysts and semiconductor absorbers used for solar water splitting. The process involves commercial hydrogen and oxygen microsensor probes and a custom photoelectrochemical cell optimized for accurate product quantification. The airtight cell consists of two identical compartments separated by an ion exchange membrane and is equipped with ports for all necessary electrodes, product detection sensors, a gas purge, and a thermocouple. Three-point calibrations are performed prior to experimentation using an inert gas purge and then injecting known volumes of hydrogen or oxygen into the cell. The technique’s accuracy is confirmed by ensuring measurements of approximately 100% faradaic efficiency for platinum and iridium electrodes for the hydrogen evolution reaction and oxygen evolution reaction, respectively (a baseline based on previous studies from the literature). The accuracy of hydrogen measurements is further confirmed using gas chromatography. Initial applications include assessing crystalline molybdenum disulfide catalysts on n + silicon wafer cathodes, which are measured to have a faradaic efficiency of 98.6%. Future work will initially focus on improving the technique’s precision and determining the effect of changing temperature on the sensors’ accuracy, after which additional catalysts and semiconductors will be evaluated, including tantalum nitride and strontium titanate photoanodes.

topic: The Oxygen Reduction Reaction on Nitrogen-Doped Graphene: A Density Functional Theory Study
title: The Oxygen Reduction Reaction on Nitrogen-Doped Graphene: A Density Functional Theory Study
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering
authors_text: Robert Warburton and Aravind Asthagiri
abstract: Increased global awareness of negative implications associated with climate change fuels the search for more sustainable forms of energy generation. Fuel cells have received considerable attention due to their efficiency, reliability, and lack of emissions. However, the sluggish kinetics of the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) remains one of the main limitations. Furthermore, current ORR catalysts use platinum, which requires a sizeable economic investment due to the high cost. Experimental work shows nitrogen-doped graphene (CN x ) catalysts operate at an overpotential similar to that of commercial platinum catalysts, but an atomic level understanding of the source of activity in these materials is still lacking. This first principles study utilizes density functional theory to model the elementary steps of the ORR on CN x materials to understand the structure-activity relationship of these materials. This study explicitly includes the role of water through inclusion of an ice-like water layer. We will discuss the impact of water on the derived overpotential of the ORR on CN x for comparison to previous work on the Pt(111). A first principles understanding of nitrogen-doped graphene activity in appropriately modeled environments will be important in efforts to improve the performance of CN x materials.

topic: Kinetic Analysis of Aqueous-Phase Pd-Catalyzed, Cu-Free Direct Arylation of Terminal Alkynes Using a Hydrophilic Ligand
title: Kinetic Analysis of Aqueous-Phase Pd-Catalyzed, Cu-Free Direct Arylation of Terminal Alkynes Using a Hydrophilic Ligand
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering
authors_text: Ria C. Domier, Jane N. Moore, Kevin H. Shaughnessy and Ryan L. Hartman
abstract: The engineering of reaction mixtures that ensure the solubility of inorganic salt byproducts without compromising the reactivity is a grand challenge for continuous flow manufacturing in upstream pharmaceuticals and fine chemicals process development. Aqueous cross-coupling reactions are possible solutions. We report the study of an aqueous phase Pd-catalyzed Cu-free direct arylation of an alkyne using a hydrophilic ligand towards understanding the role of water on the cross-coupling kinetics. Kinetic analyses of theoretically estimated molar flux rates and the measured reaction kinetics reveal a transition from mass transfer to kinetically controlled deprotonation and carbopalladation mechanisms. Interfacial contact areas of immiscible aqueous–organic phases control the crossover from the mass-transfer-limited to the reaction-rate-limited regime. Highly agitated batch reactors and multiphase capillary flow reactors are needed to overcome the mass transport limitations and, thus, discover the transition from the apparent reaction kinetics to the true reaction kinetics. Comparison of previously reported Density Functional Theory calculations with experimentally measured activation energies, ranging from 14.8 to 20.0 kcal/mol, elucidates the theoretical possibility of designing the aqueous phase C–C cross-coupling reaction with similar reactivity as purely organic reactions. Although ambiguity remains concerning which reaction step is rate-determining in either the deprotonation or the carbopalladation mechanism, our discovery undergirds that one mechanism or the other could dominate in aqueous designed direct arylations.

topic: Control of Furfural Hydrogenation Selectivity Via Modified Ni-Based Catalysts Using Self-Assembled Monolayers
title: Control of Furfural Hydrogenation Selectivity Via Modified Ni-Based Catalysts Using Self-Assembled Monolayers
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering
authors_text: Nicole Love
abstract: In a world of rising technology and limited fuel sources, the research and production of biofuels is of utmost importance. Furfural, a common component of bio-oil, is a platform chemical with the potential to create a variety of products, including an important fuel additive, methylfuran. A nickel catalyst, unlike the commonly used copper and palladium, is of interest due to its low cost despite its high reactivity and low selectivity of methylfuran. We believe that specific adsorption of furfural onto the catalyst determines its preferred reaction pathway and primary products. By adding a dense self-assembled monolayer (SAM) to the nickel catalyst surface, we can control furfural adsorption geometry, which in turn affects reaction selectivity. Experiments utilized three primary thiols: adamantanethiol (AT), octadecanethiol (C18), and 1,2-benzenedithiol (Benz). We found that benzenedithiol improved methylfuran selectivity from 10% to 88% on the pure nickel catalyst. The uncoated NiCu bimetallics decreased the selectivity of furan but did not demonstrate complete hydrodeoxygenation to methylfuran, resulting in production of furfuryl alcohol. The SAM coated bimetallics eliminated furfuryl alcohol as a product by allowing further reaction of the furfuryl alcohol to methylfuran.

topic: Catalytic Conversion of Landfill Gas to Liquid Fuel
title: Catalytic Conversion of Landfill Gas to Liquid Fuel
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering
authors_text: Ryan Kent, Devin M. Walker, Syed Ali Gardezi, Tim Roberge, Babu Joseph and John N. Kuhn
abstract: Landfill gas can be captured, converted, and used as an energy source. Approximately 234 MM tons/year of municipal solid waste is produced in United States, with the average landfill collecting 2800 ft 3 /min of landfill gas (LFG). Most of this gas is wasted by flaring while landfills spend $8,000 per day on diesel fuel for its vehicle fleet. The process involves two specialized catalysts, Ni-Mg supported on Ce 0.6 Zr 0.4 O 2 for use in a Tri-reforming reactor, turning CO 2 and methane into hydrogen and carbon monoxide (syngas). This syngas is converted using a silica eggshell catalyst in the Fischer-Tropsch reactor (FTSR). Using both the tri-reforming and the FTS reactors in tandem enables conversion of the landfill gas directly into a tailored fuel cut of middle distillates (diesel and jet fuel) without creating heavier hydrocarbons. The catalysts combat current issues of coke formation and lowers the cost of synthetic fossil fuels. The downscaling of extremely large FTS reactors is important to the implementation of this system on a wider scale. Current efforts are aimed at integration of the reactors and scaling of the prototype system.

topic: Effects of Water on Rhizopus Oryzae Whole Cell-Catalyzed Transesterification of Bean Oil for Biodiesel Production
title: Effects of Water on Rhizopus Oryzae Whole Cell-Catalyzed Transesterification of Bean Oil for Biodiesel Production
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering
authors_text: Gilda Naka and Qiyang He
abstract: Effects of water on Rhizopus oryzae whole cell-catalyzed transesterification of bean oil for biodiesel production * Gilda Naka a , Qiyang He b a REU program, Alabama Agricultural and Mechanical University, Normal, AL, USA b Department of Chemical Engineering, Nanjing Forestry University, Nanjing, Jiangsu, China 11 July 2013 *All documentation and findings are property of Alabama A&M University, Nanjing Forestry University, and the authors listed above. __________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Abstract Biodiesel produced by the methanolysis of plant oils has received a lot of research attention due to its potential as a renewable and environmentally-friendly energy resource. The use of a whole-cell biocatalyst eliminates the need for purification that is necessary for most modern industrial processes and appears to be a more efficient and promising technique in the process of producing biofuel through the transesterfication of triglycerides. The effect of water on biodiesel production was investigated with the use of bean oil and Rhizopus oryzae whole cell with polyurethane foaming plastic as a whole-cell biocatalyst. The optimal water content was found to be 10% after 60 hours. The results presented could be beneficial for developing an efficient and cost-effective biodiesel production technique.

title: Photocatalytic Activity Enhancement of Titania By Addition of Plasmonic Ag Nanocubes
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering
authors_text: Jon Pickering, Venkat R. Bhethanabotla and John N. Kuhn
abstract: Optically active Ag nanocubes were combined with TiO2 to form a model composite material to study the conditions at which the photochemical activity of TiO2 is enhanced via plasmonics. Using varying compositions of the composite material, the photocatalytic degradation of methyl orange under ultraviolet and “day-light” spectrum irradiation was measured using UV-Vis spectroscopy. Interpretation of the results has aided in determining the conditions at which the plasmonic properties of the Ag nanocubes can enhance the system.

topic: Kinetics of 2,3-Butanediol Reaction with Cu-ZSM-5 (23)
title: Kinetics of 2,3-Butanediol Reaction with Cu-ZSM-5 (23)
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering
authors_text: Lara McDougald, Keith L. Hohn and Quanxing Zheng
abstract: The rising costs and harmful environmental impacts of fossil fuels has made developing renewable energies very important. Through bacterial fermentation, biomass can be converted into 2 ,3 -butanediol (2,3-BDO). Using a bifunctional catalyst to catalyze both a hydrogenation and dehydration reaction, 2 ,3 -BDO can be converted in butene, which can then be used as a jet additive. In this study, the kinetics of the 2 ,3 -BDO reaction with catalyst Cu-ZSM-5 (23) was investigated using a small-scale batch reactor. The reaction was run at various reaction times, temperatures, and with or without hydrogen gas present. The liquid products were analyzed using a gas chromatography mass spectrometer. The gas phase was studied using a thermal conductivity detector and flame ionization detector. By identifying the types and amounts of products made, a new reaction mechanism was proposed for the conversion of 2 ,3 -butanediol into butene. This mechanism is shown in Figure 1. The butadiene pathway seemed to be favored over the pathway involving the formation of propanol. Hydrogen was seen as a byproduct of the reaction. More tests should be done on this reaction to further modify the mechanism. Determining an accurate reaction mechanism is important to designing a catalyst that will best optimize the production of butene and make its production cost competitive with petroleum based butene. Figure 1. Proposed mechanism of 2 ,3 -butanediol conversion to butene using Cu-ZSM-5 (23) catalyst.

topic: Adsorption Studies of Biomass-Derived Molecules in HY and NaY Zeolites By Quantum Mechanics/Molecular Mechanics Calculations
title: Adsorption Studies of Biomass-Derived Molecules in HY and NaY Zeolites By Quantum Mechanics/Molecular Mechanics Calculations
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering
authors_text: Shuting Feng, Tim Courtney, Stavros Caratzoulas and Dionisios G. Vlachos
abstract: An embedded-cluster model and Density Functional Theory (DFT) are employed to investigate the adsorption energy of unsaturated aliphatic, aromatic and heterocyclic compounds in HY and NaY zeolites. The quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) ONIOM method is used to model the catalytically active site and the surrounding zeolitic environment, and the results are calculated using the Gaussian 09 computational package and compared to those calculated by Nikbin et al. 1 using a quantum cluster. Our results show that 1) ethylene exhibits the weakest binding among all adsorbates considered in both zeolites, regardless of the cluster models and basis sets employed; 2) in HY zeolite, the quantum cluster calculations predict comparable binding energies of oxa-norbornene and p-xylene, while the QM/MM calculations predict significantly higher binding energy of oxa-norbornene than that of p-xylene; 3) in NaY zeolite, both the quantum cluster and the ONIOM scheme predict very similar binding energies of oxa-norbornene and p-xylene, regardless of the cluster models and basis sets used; 4) smaller clusters tend to underestimate the binding energy; 5) the QM/MM methodology is very sensitive to the choice of cluster size and basis set, as the use of different cluster models and basis sets can contribute to differences of more than 7 kcal/mol and 5 kcal/mol in binding energy, respectively; 6) the parallel configuration of ethylene and DMF co-adsorption in HY zeolite was found to have much higher adsorption energy than the vertical configuration. Reference 1. Nikbin, N.; Caratzoulas, S.; Vlachos, D. G. (submitted to J. Catal)

topic: New Solid Acid Catalyst for Brown Grease Biodiesel Production
title: New Solid Acid Catalyst for Brown Grease Biodiesel Production
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering
authors_text: Alex Lavernoich, Iman Noshadi, Baishali Kanjilal and Richard Parnas
abstract: There is a big movement in our country to turn many of our processes more sustainable and environmentally friendly. Alternative fuels have started to play a role in this, with ethanol and biodiesel being added to regular petroleum based gasses to help decrease their environmental impact. Biodiesel is created when fats and other carbon chains are reacted with small chained alcohols. Biodiesel is currently made from various vegetable oils and “yellow grease”, used kitchen oils that contain slight amounts of fatty acids, but still easily converted to biodiesel. But another form of grease, brown grease, can also be used to make biodiesel. Brown grease commonly refers to sewer and water treatment waste that contains 50-100% FFA (free fatty acids). Currently brown grease is disposed of by dumping it in landfills or incinerating it. Neither of the methods are particularly environmentally friendly since the heavy metals trapped in the grease either leak into the land or get released into the air when incinerated. But if the oil layers of brown grease were to be converted into biodiesel, the stress the waste causes on our environment would lessen and a usable resource would be created. Brown grease cannot be prepared in the same way as vegetable oils and “yellow grease” due to the high content of FFA. When triglyceride rich oils are converted a base catalyst is used as transesterification happens quicker in the presence of a base then in the presence of an acid. But if FFA is reacted in the presence of a base, any ions or impurities in the brown grease will cause saponification instead of esterification, and soap instead of biodiesel will be created. So esterification is generally done with an acid as a catalyst. The most common catalysts for esterification are the readily available hydrochloric acid and sulfuric acid. Both of the acids are liquids and get washed away when the biodiesel is cleaned with water, so each time new catalyst must be used. A solid acid catalyst theoretically would be able to catalyze the reaction and be reusable through several reactions since it can be easily separated and retained. A new acid catalyst (OMR-[C 4 HMTA][SO 4 H]) was made from the self-assembly of resol precursors, hexamethylenetetramine (HMTA) cross-linker, and a tri-block copolymer template of Pluronic® F127 (Sigma-Aldrich) (Scheme 1). This created the OMR-[HMTA] backbone which when reacted with 1,4-butanesultone, forms OMR-[C 4 HMTA][SO 4 H]. This catalyst was made in lab to compare to the commercially available Amberlyst 15 solid acid and the commonly used non-reusable hydrochloric acid. When the physical proportions of our catalyst was compared to that of the Amberlyst 15, the OMR-[C 4 HMTA][SO 4 H] had a larger BET surface area and a larger pore volume. This would suggest that it would be better for reacting with more of the catalyst being available to use per mass. Two treatments of the brown grease were tested to compare the catalysts. The first process starts with 20 mL of brown grease that is reacted with excess methanol and 5% weight with respect to oil of catalyst at 65°C until there was under 1% FFA by looking at the acid number found using a 0.07 M potassium hydroxide titration using ASTM Method D6751. After the first reaction, the sample was centrifuged to separate any solid catalyst from the oil/biodiesel sample, and then the sample was washed with distilled water then dried by bubbling air through it. The sample was then put into a new reactor with excess methanol and 5% (w/w) of KOH at 65°C for one hour to convert the glyceride portions of the grease to biodiesel. The second way to treat the sample was to try and have esterification and transesterification happen in one step. 10 g of brown grease oil was reacted with a methanol and the acid catalysts for 5 hours at 65°C. The methanol/oil had about a 40:1 molar ratio (excess), and the catalyst/oil mass ratio was .05:1. Each catalyst was tested under the same conditions above, and for just esterification, the OMR-[C 4 HMTA][SO 4 H] ended up converting about 99.5% of the FFA to biodiesel after only 1.5 hours. Both Amberlyst 15 and HCl on the other hand had less than a 98% conversion of FFA after 8 hours. When the one step esterification and transesterification was done, OMR-[C 4 HMTA][SO 4 H] ended up converting about 75% of the triglycerides to biodiesel after 5 hours, which ended up being the equilibrium. The other catalysts ended up converting less than 65% of the triglycerides after a 5 hour period. While the triglyceride conversion was very good for an acid catalyzed transesterification, the final biodiesel just missed passing the ASTM D 6751 specifications because of a too high level of total glycerin in the fuel. The mesporous solid acid catalyst proved to be extremely reactive for the esterification of FFA in brown grease, and when transesterification was done with KOH after the final biodiesel product passed all ASTM quality checks.

topic: Composition-Activity Correlation of Gold-Supported Nickel Cobalt Cerium Catalyst for Electrochemical Oxygen Evolution
title: Composition-Activity Correlation of Gold-Supported Nickel Cobalt Cerium Catalyst for Electrochemical Oxygen Evolution
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering
authors_text: Woo Yong Choi, Yun Cai and Alexis T. Bell
abstract: Inspired by natural photosynthesis, artificial photosynthesis is a promising renewable energy technology that produces valuable fuel from water, carbon dioxide and sunlight with no CO 2 emissions. The competence of this technology depends heavily on the catalysts for oxygen evolution reaction (OER). The catalysts must have a low overpotential, consist of earth-abundant materials, and be durable to corrosion. We now report the superior performance and stability of novel Ni-Co-Ce ternary heterogeneous catalyst electrodeposited on gold substrate. Activity versus correlation study of Ni-Co-Ce has been conducted using various electrochemistry techniques and Inductive Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (ICP-MS). All electrochemical studies were done in 1.0M KOH at room temperature. Activity studies showed that certain compositions of Ni-Co-Ce catalysts demonstrated overpotentials as low as 270mV. In addition to its high catalytic efficiency, stable performance for over two hours was demonstrated through stability tests. ICP-MS tests verified the actual catalyst film composition, as opposed to electrolyte composition, and revealed that the activity depends closely with Ce composition. This study establishes the basis for further mechanistic studies and scale up of artificial photosynthesis technology.

topic: Hydrogen Production from Solar Water Splitting
title: Hydrogen Production from Solar Water Splitting
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering
authors_text: Faidy Rusinque
abstract: H 2 Production from Solar Water Splitting Faidy Rusinque Mentor: Xianqin Wang New Jersey Institute of Technology Newark, NJ Abstract: In the last few years there has been an intensive research focused on alternative H 2 production technologies. Solar to-Hydrogen conversion methods such as photocatalytic water splitting need to be developed so that the transition to a hydrogen-based energy infrastructure can be made effortlessly. Producing hydrogen from water with tunable band gap of TiO 2 will resolve several issues: Proper utilization of the solar energy spectrum, clean hydrogen production, and minimization of CO 2 emissions. TiO 2 is perhaps the most promising semiconductor material due to its effectiveness for harnessing solar energy for H 2 generation. In this study we determined H 2 production activities over a series of TiO 2 -based catalysts from solar water splitting. We investigated the correlation between TiO 2 properties with the hydrogen production activities by tuning particle size, TiO 2 surface areas, and different metal (Pt) loading on TiO 2 . TiO 2 -based catalysts were synthesized with incipient impregnation method and characterized with CO chemisorption, temperature programmed reduction and desorption, surface area measurements at liquid nitrogen temperature, powder XRD patterns, and activity measurements. The activity results showed that the TiO 2 surface area, metal dispersion and particle size affect the H 2 Production rate.

topic: Alcohol Dehydration over Zr-KIT-6: Lewis Acidic Zr-Incorporated Mesoporous Silicates
title: Alcohol Dehydration over Zr-KIT-6: Lewis Acidic Zr-Incorporated Mesoporous Silicates
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering
authors_text: Jason Bates, Qing Pan, Anand Ramanathan and Bala Subramanian
abstract: Dehydration of alcohols over a solid acid catalyst is a key step in producing alkenes from bioalcohols obtained by fermentation and C-C coupling using either Guerbet synthesis or hydroformylation. The common solid acid catalysts used for dehydration in industry are zeolites [1]. However, their microporous structure induces pore diffusion limitations with either progressively longer chain alcohols or sugar alcohols such as glycerol, rendering them susceptible to deactivation by fouling [2]. MCM-type zeolites with a mesoporous structure have been attempted to address this problem [3], but low hydrothermal stability and structural reproducibility are significant drawbacks [4]. To address these disadvantages, we have developed a solid Lewis acidic catalyst with a tunable pore size by incorporating Zr into the mesoporous silicate structure KIT-6. Characterization of the catalyst shows a narrow pore size distribution (with mean pore size ~7 nm) with a high number of medium-strength acid sites depending on Zr content [4]. Zr-KIT-6 has been tested for dehydration of linear C 2 -C 4 alcohols. In the 190-300 °C temperature range, the Zr-KIT-6 catalysts showed > 98% selectivity to propene. The intrinsic rate constants obtained in the absence of mass transfer limitations scale with the number of acid sites in the various Zr-KIT-6 samples. The intrinsic activation energy was ~49 kJ/mol and the catalyst activity was stable for several days during continuous runs in a fixed-bed reactor [5]. These results along with those from the dehydration of other alcohols such as ethanol will be presented. References 1. Tanabe, K., Hölderich, W.F., 1999. topic: Multi-Enzyme Colocalization on Nanocarriers for Investigating Biosynthesis
title: Multi-Enzyme Colocalization on Nanocarriers for Investigating Biosynthesis
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering
authors_text: Louai Labanieh
abstract: Many cascaded biological reactions are catalyzed by enzymes that exist as multi-enzyme complexes. The spatial colocalization of enzymes in these complexes increases the reaction efficiency by ensuring that the reactive intermediates have rapid access to neighboring active sites and maintaining high local concentrations. Although some work has been done on colocalizing model enzymes, there is a lack of knowledge regarding less robust enzymes. Inspired by nature, we immobilized and colocalized two diterpene synthases (DTS) that catalyze the production of sclareol, a valuable fragrance prized in the perfume industry, onto polymeric and nonpolymeric nanoparticles (NPs). Colocalization of DTS enzymes onto NPs can increase the reaction efficiency by producing local environments that facilitate the catalysis of sclareol. The immobilization of these enzymes onto a NP can also improve their stability. Our strategy for immobilization was designed for the binding of histidine-tagged enzymes on to nickel nitrilotriacetic acid-functionalized NPs. We investigated the binding efficiency and retained catalytic activity of the enzyme-nanoparticle conjugates for silica NPs (SiNPs), polystyrene NPs, and gold NPs. We achieved significant binding for SiNPs, but there was little retained catalytic activity (1.1%). Polystyrene NPs also bound a substantial amount of enzymes, but sclareol production could not be determined because these NPs interfered with our hexane extraction process. Gold nanoparticles did not disrupt the activity of the enzyme, but the high cost of this material made it prohibitively expensive to procure quantities that would load a substantial amount of enzymes. An ideal nanocarrier will be one that yields a high binding capacity while retaining the catalytic activity of the loaded enzymes and should be amenable to quantitative assays and extractions.

topic: The Effect of Co-Solvent & Ordered Lattice Structure on Catalysis of Biodiesel Production in Microreactors
title: The Effect of Co-Solvent & Ordered Lattice Structure on Catalysis of Biodiesel Production in Microreactors
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering
authors_text: Ben Kegley and Dr. Frank Jones
abstract: In this study, microreactors are used to make fatty acid methyl esters (biodiesel). Microreactors have many advantages over traditional reaction systems due to scale. Benefits include an increase in product purity and a reduction of processing time from hours to seconds. Microfluidic channel size is 50 µm by 500 µm with length of 3 to 15 cm. The channels are coated with a metal base catalyst, Nickel (II) Oxide. This metal catalyst converts a wide variety of vegetable oils to biodiesel. Also, typical feedstock impurities, such as free fatty acids, are successfully converted to biodiesel. Variations in temperature, feedstock composition, and the multiphase nature of the feedstock are also being investigated. Microreactors, in this study, have already successfully produced levels of conversion equivalent to stirred tank systems while reducing hours of processing time to minutes. Additionally, adding free fatty acid to the SBO/methanol feed as a co-solvent, reducing processing fluid to a single phase, has already increased initial global rates. Currently, further design improvements, such as increased catalyst surface coverage and the introduction of ordered lattice structures, are being employed in order to reduce processing time to seconds.

topic: Insights into Dehydration of 1,2,6-Hexanetriol over Model Silica-Alumina Surfaces
title: Insights into Dehydration of 1,2,6-Hexanetriol over Model Silica-Alumina Surfaces
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering
authors_text: Jung Youn Cho, Matthew Neurock, Qiaohua Tan, Michael Nolan and Brent H. Shanks
abstract: Increasing interests in the use of biorenewables feedstocks as alternatives to petroleum sources have promoted many of the recent studies in the literature on the dehydration, hydrogenolysis, decarbonylation and decarboxylation pathways of oxygenated intermediates derived from biomass. The selective dehydration and functionalization of polyols such as 1,2,6-hexanetriol to α,ω-diols are important paths that may enable the production of diacids, diamines, and lactones from renewable sources. Herein we use first-principle theoretical calculations to examine the reaction paths and mechanism involved in the dehydration of 1,2,6-hexanetriol over model silica alumina catalytic surfaces. More specifically, we carry out density function theory (DFT) calculations to examine the reaction pathways and elementary steps in the dehydration of 1,2,6-hexanetriol over a model 2D zeolite structures. Experimental results reported by Nolan and Shanks at ISU show significantly higher selectivities for the conversion of 1,2,6-hexanetriol to THP-2-M than to the more desired 6-hydroxyhexanal product. The results from theoretical calculations indicate that the intrinsic activation barriers for the formation of THP-2-M is 72 kJ/mol whereas the barrier to form 6-hydroxyhexanal is 84 kJ/mol (12 kJ/mol higher) which is consistent with the much higher selectivities to the THP-2-M product reported experimentally. The reaction of 1,2,6-hexanetriol to the THP-2-M proceeds via the protonation and elimination of the OH group at the 2-position of the triol to form a secondary carbenium ion that is stabilized by the direct interaction with the primary OH group at the 6-position to form a stable 6-member ring carbenium ion intermediate. The reaction of 1,2,6-hexanetriol to form the 6-hydroxyhexanal product also proceeds via the protonation and elimination of the OH group at the 2-position. The secondary carbenium ion that forms, however, is now stabilized by a hydride transfer from the 1- to the 2- position on the triol in order to localize the charge on the terminal OH group. DFT calculations were carried out on all of the other viable dehydration paths including the dehydration of the terminal OH groups at the 1- and 6-positions. The dehydration barriers at the primary 1- and 6- positions of 1,2,6-hexanetriol were all calculated to be at least 9 kJ/mol higher than those at the secondary position. The theoretical results also showed that 1,6 hexanediol can be formed via the dehydration of the primary OH groups along with an OH shift from the secondary carbon to the terminal carbon but requires significantly higher activation barriers. The main paths to THP-2-M and 6-hydroxyhexanal products were thus concluded to occur via the dehydration of the secondary OH intermediate. Theoretical results also indicate that the production of oxepan-3-ol is also possible via the dehydration of both of the terminal 1- and 6- OH species to form oxepan-3-ol with a barrier of 88 kJ/mol which is 16 kJ/mol higher than that to form THP-2-M. Finally, the ring opening of THP-2-M to hexanal was calculated to be 130 kJ/mol which indicates that THP-2-M is quite stable and does not react further which is consistent with the high selectivities measured experimentally. The mechanistic insights gleaned from this work help to advance our knowledge for the dehydration of polyols found in most biorenewables feeds and can be used to help to provide a more general understanding of the dehydrogenation reaction of polyols over acid catalysts.

topic: An Operando Molecular Spectroscopic and DFT Calculation Investigation of Methane Aromatization By Supported Mo/ZSM-5 Catalysts
title: An Operando Molecular Spectroscopic and DFT Calculation Investigation of Methane Aromatization By Supported Mo/ZSM-5 Catalysts
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering
authors_text: Juliana Telles and Yadan Tang
abstract: An Operando Molecular Spectroscopic and DFT Calculation Investigation of Methane Aromatization by Supported Mo/ZSM-5 Catalysts The recent discovery of abundant shell gas has renewed interest in conversion of gas to liquids technology (GTL). The GTL technology has the potential to convert a significant percentage of natural gas into liquid petroleum enough to supply the world’s energy needs for the next 25 years. In addition to natural gas, large amounts of methane are available from coal beds and as byproducts of petroleum refining. The relative inertness of CH 4 has limited its application as chemical feedstock in spite of the relative abundance of this inexpensive hydrocarbon. It has been estimated that the methane byproduct being flared from crude oil fields is equivalent to about 1 million barrels of oil per day. Consequently, a long term research goal is the upgrading of methane into higher molecular weight hydrocarbons that are economically more valuable, more easily transportable or stored, and can be suitable feed stocks for current commercial petrochemical manufacturing processes. According to the assessment from Honeywell (UOP), the production of synthesis gas (syngas, consisting of a mixture of CO and H 2 ) is 80% of the cost of the indirect GTL process. Therefore, a more effective process which can avoid the production of syngas is explored. The direct route such as direct non-oxidative conversion of methane to aromatics (benzene and naphthalene) emerges. The most promising catalyst is the supported Mo/ZSM-5 catalyst for non-oxidative conversion of methane to aromatics. Supported molybdenum oxide catalysts are widely employed as commercial catalysts for hyrodesulfurization and hydrocracking of heavy fractions of crude oil, olefin metathesis, isomerization, hydrogenation and polymerization of alkenes in the petroleum industry, and partial oxidation of aliphatic alcohols 5 . The ZSM-5 is a type of aluminosilicate zeolite patented by Mobil which has a pore opening of about 5.5 Å in size similar to the size of a benzene molecule. It has been widely used in the petroleum industry as a heterogeneous catalyst for hydrocarbon isomerization reactions. The pioneering work of the activity of Mo/ZSM-5 catalysts in dehydro-aromatization of methane was reported by Wang 1 in 1993. Their supported Mo/ZSM-5 catalyst exhibited a high selectivity for methane towards benzene. Many researchers have reported the optimum catalytic activity of 7~ 12% CH 4 conversion and 70~100% selectivity towards benzene over Mo/ZSM-5 catalysts with 2~3 wt% molybdenum loading 1-4 . Supported Mo/ZSM-5 catalysts are able to convert methane to aromatics, but despite intensive studies there is no agreement in the catalysis literature about: the nature of supported Mo species on ZSM-5 (monomer, dimer or cluster) and anchoring site(s) of Mo species (Al-Al, Al-Si or Si-Si). The intense interest in supported molybdena catalysts has motivated numerous molecular structural characterization studies of the surface MoOx species: in situ Raman 6,7,8 , infrared (IR) 9, 10 , in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 x-ray absorption spectroscopy (XANES/EXAFS) 14 , temperature programmed desorption (TPD)/temperature programmed reduction (TPR) 15 , X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) 16 , and UV-visible diffuse reflectance spectroscopy (DRS) 16, 17 . These characterization investigations have significantly contributed to the fundamental understanding of supported molybdena catalysts and impacted both their fundamental research and industrial development efforts. In situ UV-vis DRS revealed that the initial supported MoO x are exclusively present as isolated monomeric surface sites on the ZSM-5 support. Combined in situ Raman spectroscopy and DFT calculations in H 2 18 O exchange, dehydrated Raman, and H 2 –TPR experiments, however, revealed the presence of four distinct surface MoO x structures on the Mo/ZSM-5 support: 1) isolated dioxo (O=) 2 MoO 2 surface site over two Brønsted acid sites at low Mo loading and high Al content at 998 cm -1 ; 2) isolated dioxo (O=) 2 MoO 2 surface site over one Brønsted acid site and an adjacent Si-OH group at increasing Mo loading at 970 cm -1 ; 3) isolated dioxo (O=) 2 MoO 2 surface site over two Si-OH groups at low Al content at 983 cm -1 ; 4) isolated mono-oxo O=MoO 4 surface site over extra framework Al-OH groups at high Al content found at 1026 cm -1 . In situ FT-IR showed that MoO x prefers to anchor at Brønsted acid sites at low Mo loading, and at Si-OH and external Al-OH groups at higher Mo loading and low Al content. The addition of MoO x to ZSM-5 also indicates dealumination and forms extra-framework Al 2 O 3 NPs. These new studies demonstrate how systematic studies with modern approaches to catalysis research are able to resolve the fundamental issues of complex catalytic systems and establish the relationships between the molecular and electronic structures of the catalytic active sites and the corresponding catalytic activity and selectivity performance. topic: Controlled Nucleation and Overgrowth of Platinum on Silver Nanoparticles
title: Controlled Nucleation and Overgrowth of Platinum on Silver Nanoparticles
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering
authors_text: Julie Nguyen, Matthew Kale and Phillip Christopher
abstract: Controlled nucleation and overgrowth of platinum on silver nanoparticles Traditional catalytic processes are primarily driven by thermal energy derived from fossil fuels, which is not sustainable or energy efficient. An alternative option would be to captivate the energy released from the sun. The conversion of solar energy to chemical energy is an uprising innovation to drive selective chemical processes. The storage of energy in chemical bonds through visible light positively leads to the remission of pollution and overcomes many of the limitations of fossil fuels. Metallic nanoparticles, which exhibit a unique interaction with visible light, can be synthesized with different geometries and optimized optical properties. In this work, we show that bimetallic nanoparticles with engineered photocatalytic and optical properties can be optimized through the control of nanoparticle geometry, rates of metal precursor addition, concentration of reducing agents, and weight loading. These bimetallic nanostructures will be tested for thermal and photothermal reactivity to show that they can be utilized for the efficient conversion of solar energy into chemical bonds.

topic: The Effect Of InVO 4 Coupling On The Photocatalytic Activity Of Anatase and Mixed Phase TiO 2 For Organic Decomposition
title: The Effect Of InVO 4 Coupling On The Photocatalytic Activity Of Anatase and Mixed Phase TiO 2 For Organic Decomposition
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering
authors_text: Cheryl H. McCane, Sandra L. Pettit and John N. Kuhn
abstract: To increase sustainability of water systems, focus must be turned to the removal of persistent contaminants, including dyes, pesticides, and cyanobacterial metabolites. Photocatalysis, an Advanced Oxidation Process, has greater potential for treating persistent organic contaminants than traditional methods such as chlorine and potassium permanganate. TiO 2 is an effective, inexpensive, and stable photocatalyst used for the decomposition of organics, however; it is limited by its band gap (3.0-3.2 eV) which primarily absorbs in the ultraviolet portion of the spectrum. This project is innovative because it will use the indium vanadate semiconductor, InVO 4 , alloyed to TiO 2 , to increase visible range photoactivity. TiO 2 occurs in several crystalline phases (e.g. anatase, rutile, and brookite).The objective of this study was to determine if the effect on photoactivity of InVO 4 alloying was consistent for pure phase and mixed phase TiO 2 . Pure anatase and mixed phase TiO 2­ (Degussa P25) were used. Batch reactions were carried out at atmospheric pressure and ambient temperature in 1-L pyrex reactors stirred at 250 rpm. The light source was “Daylight Spectrum” florescent bulbs. Photocatalytic activity was determined by monitoring methyl orange concentration using UV-Vis analysis at 15 min intervals. From the data collected, the effect of InVO 4 coupling on the photoactivity was not consistent between anatase and P25 TiO 2­ . Decomposition by the anatase composite was retarded, but decomposition by the mixed phase composite was enhanced. Although these results were unexpected, current research implicates decomposition may occur via two different mechanisms, which may explain why the coupling of InVO 4 affected the phases differently.
